## The Museum of Almost

The museum had no sign.

It occupied the back room of a former bakery on Bell Street, between a locksmith and a shop that sold only houseplants. Its hours were posted in handwritten letters behind the glass door: **Open when we are here. Closed when we are not.**

This was a misleading notice, according to Veda, who had founded the museum and served as its only curator.

“Most places are closed when they’re empty,” she explained to visitors. “We’re the opposite.”

The museum contained things that had almost happened.

There was a train ticket to a town its owner had never visited. A silver earring missing its partner. A letter begun so carefully that the first line filled an entire page: *I know you will think this is strange, but—*

There were two coffee cups from a café that had burned down six years ago. A child’s shoe without its mate. A pair of sunglasses through which no one could remember looking. A key so old that its original lock had been replaced three times.

Each object had a card explaining what it might have become.

**GUARD: I almost became a surgeon.**

**HANDWRITTEN CARD: I almost said I was sorry.**

**TICKET TO LARKSPUR: I almost went home.**

Not everything was dramatic. Veda liked the ordinary things best. A button. A bus timetable. A peach pit. Things that had brushed against a life and might have altered it, had someone looked closer.

“Why keep the things that didn’t happen?” a boy asked her once.

“They still mattered,” Veda said.

“To who?”

“To whoever almost did.”

On the afternoon I came to work, a little girl was standing before an empty shelf.

She was perhaps five. Her red boots shone beneath her coat, and she held one hand behind her back, as if concealing evidence.

“What happened to this one?” she asked.

“It was never found,” I told her.

Her face fell. “Oh.”

Veda came from the storeroom, brushing flour from her sleeves. The museum had been hers for eleven years, though she was vague about what she had done before that. “It isn’t missing,” she said gently. “It’s just an almost.”

The girl considered this.

“What are you looking for?”

“Nothing,” she said. “I just like knowing where it is.”

We laughed, and she laughed too, embarrassed by her own solemnity. Then she reached behind her back and produced a single white button.

“I found this in the park,” she said. “It doesn’t have a coat.”

Veda crouched down. The button was smooth and ordinary, the kind of thing nobody notices until it falls off.

“You could make a museum for it,” the girl said.

“We already have,” Veda replied.

Years later, the museum acquired a larger building. Veda added wings for lost directions, unwritten songs, and all the people who had boarded trains but stepped back onto the platform. The empty shelves multiplied. The city began sending us things in blue boxes, packed carefully between layers of newspaper.

I stayed to help Veda catalogue the collection.

On my first evening as curator, after the last visitor had gone, I found a ticket on the front desk.

It was creased into quarters and softened at the edges. Someone had written a name on the back, then crossed it out. Beneath the name, in small letters, were three words:

**ALMOST STAYED.**

I carried the ticket into the exhibition hall. There was an empty case by the window, its label blank.

I placed the ticket inside.

Then I locked the door and watched the streetlights flicker on, one by one, along Bell Street.
